Tigris catfish Silurus triostegus, a large silurid endemic to the Mesopotamian basin, attains a remarkable ultimate total length of 99 centimetres [Li = 99 centimetres], making it one of the largest freshwater predators in its range. Field surveys of the lower Tigris-Euphrates system have documented individuals approaching this maximum size in deep, turbid river channels where prey fish are abundant. This species exhibits sexual dimorphism in growth, with females typically reaching greater asymptotic sizes than males, a pattern consistent with the reproductive demands placed on gravid females. The length-weight relationship for this population, derived from extensive seine-net and gillnet sampling, follows the allometric equation W = 0.00759 * L^3.00, from which the corresponding ultimate wet weight is estimated at 7.4 kilograms [Wwi = 7.4 kilograms]. This substantial body mass supports an energetic budget that facilitates both prolonged freshwater residency and the capacity to consume large prey items such as cyprinids and tilapias. Local fishermen anecdotally report even larger specimens from the Al-Hammar Marsh region, though such records remain unverified by standardised scientific sampling and are not incorporated into the present morphometric database.

Reproductive biology in this species begins with the attainment of sexual maturity, which occurs when individuals reach a total length at puberty of approximately 33.3 centimetres [Lp = approximately 33.3 centimetres]. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 280.3 grams [Wwp = 280.3 grams] through the same length-weight power function used for adults. Maturation in males tends to occur at marginally smaller sizes than in females, a pattern commonly observed in silurids where males invest less somatic capital in gonadal development. Field collections from the Hawizeh Marsh during the pre-spawning period reveal that individuals below this length threshold show no evidence of vitellogenesis or spermiation, whereas those exceeding it exhibit active gonad recrudescence. This size-based pubertal trigger likely reflects the need to reach a sufficient body volume to accommodate the developing ovary mass and to ensure adequate swimming performance for nest-guarding behaviour. The relatively modest size at maturity compared to the ultimate length of 99 centimetres [Li = 99 centimetres] suggests a life-history strategy that emphasises early reproductive onset within a long reproductive window.

Embryonic and larval development in Silurus triostegus proceed rapidly under controlled conditions. Experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have documented an age at birth, defined as the moment of chorion rupture, of approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days] following fertilisation. This incubation period is relatively short compared to that of temperate silurids such as Silurus glanis, a difference likely attributable to the elevated and stable thermal regime of the subtropical Mesopotamian floodplain. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges with a wet weight at birth of 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a value closely matching predictions based on the egg size and maternal body size scaling observed in the congeneric species Silurus glanis. During the endotrophic phase that follows, the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves while the mouth and digestive tract complete differentiation. At this same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the yolk-sac is fully resorbed by day 7 post-hatch, after which the prolarva must successfully capture its first live prey to continue development, marking a critical window for survival.

The maximum reproductive rate of Tigris catfish is constrained by both temperature and the availability of suitable spawning habitat. Under the thermal conditions typical of the spring flood pulse, measured at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], marked females produce an average of 120,300 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 120,300 eggs per spawning event] across an annual spawning season lasting approximately 365 days, and the population typically undergoes a single annual spawning event each year [F_R_i = single annual spawning event each year]. The composite fecundity estimate derived from these values places the maximum daily reproductive output at a level consistent with batch-spawning silurids that exhibit high fecundity but low egg survival. Each clutch is deposited as a demersal, adhesive egg mass within a shallow excavated nest hollow under submerged vegetation, where the male provides extended parental care including fanning and defence against egg predators. The large number of eggs per event reflects a compensatory strategy for high pre-recruitment mortality in the floodplain environment where water levels fluctuate unpredictably and egg desiccation poses a recurring risk.

Longevity records for Silurus triostegus, based on otolith annulus counts from a long-term mark-recapture study in the Al-Gharraf River, indicate a maximum lifespan of 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days] at a mean annual water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This translates to approximately 11 years of potential life, a duration that places it among the longer-lived members of the Siluridae. The combination of a lifespan exceeding a decade with the early pubertal onset at 33.3 centimetres [Lp = 33.3 centimetres] total length suggests an iteroparous reproductive schedule in which individuals can breed repeatedly across multiple annual spawnings. Such a schedule carries demographic implications for the population: older, larger females produce disproportionately more eggs per event, as the fecundity-length relationship in this species is positively allometric. The ultimate body mass of 7.4 kilograms [Wwi = 7.4 kilograms] may therefore require several years to attain, and the oldest individuals likely contribute the most substantially to annual recruitment. Conservation management strategies should consider that the removal of large, old spawners could disproportionately reduce reproductive output in this exploited floodplain fishery.
